newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais says privatisation not too costly.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais says privatisation not too costly.

text.p: French bank Credit Lyonnais said on Wednesday it would need less than five billion francs ($858.9 million) to be privatised and the state would reap much more than that from the sale.
"The state would be able to give the final lick of paint to the bank for less than five billion francs," chairman Jean Peyrelevade told the newspaper La Provence.

The bank, which nearly collapsed in the early 1990s under the weight of an ill-fated lending spree, confirmed on Thursday the contents of the interview, carried out before the June 1 parliamentary election which swept the left to power.
The Socialist-led government has put privatisations on hold.
Peyrelevade estimated that the state would get between 20 billion and 25 billion francs from privatisation of the bank, which is 80 percent state-owned.
"I estimate the proceeds from the privatisation at between 20 and 25 billion francs, very significantly higher than this financial effort," he said.
Peyrelevade, who has links with the Socialists as a one-time top aide to former Socialist prime minister Pierre Mauroy, said privatisation was the only way forward for the bank.
He said he did not believe the election of the Socialists would stand in the way of privatisation of the bank promised by the previous conservative government.
"I don't think that's really going to up-end things" he said. "Privatisation is the only solution for Credit Lyonnais."
But he said he did not see a sell-off before the end of 1998.
"We need to be sufficiently prosperous which is not yet the case. These conditions will certainly not be in place before the end of 1998," he said.
The five billion franc sum is way below the 12 billion francs Peyrelevade originally suggested the bank might need to boost its solvency ratios to attract a buyer.

The bank has staged an unexpectedly strong recovery. Analysts expect it to have profits of around 1.3 billion francs this year and 2.4 billion in 1998. Credit Lyonnais posted a profit of 202 million francs in 1996 after limping back to the black in 1995 with a profit of 13 million francs.
It lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994.

The cost to taxpayers from Credit Lyonnais' runaway expansion carried out when the Socialists were previously in power is likely to exceed 100 billion francs and could hit 150 billion, according to some estimates.

After numerous delays, the conservative government and Credit Lyonnais reached agreement last month on a plan to privatise the bank which was due to be submitted to the European Commission for approval.
It is not known whether the new government will want to redraft the plan which involves disposal of most of the bank's European assets outside France to meet EU conditions for approval of state aid.

The bank needs the Commission's approval for a decision by the previous government to neutralise the cost of a loan granted by the bank under a previous state bailout. That loan was needed to fund the cost of selling off shaky assets. ($ = 5.821 French Francs)
